title: Grandchild's voice: “I'm in trouble”
setup: Late at night, your phone rings. The voice sounds exactly like your grandson, and he's crying.

messages.text: It's me, I'm in trouble. I got in a car accident and they arrested me. Please don't tell Mom.
(A new voice) I'm his attorney. Bail is $4,000. A courier can pick up cash from your home tonight so he isn't held over the weekend.

options.label: Get the cash ready for the courier
options.feedback: The voice was cloned with AI from videos online. Your grandson was asleep at home.

options.label: Hang up and call your grandson or his parents on a number you know
options.feedback: Calling a number you already have exposes the fake in seconds. Voices can be cloned from a short clip.

options.label: Ask the caller a question only your grandson would know
options.feedback: A private question (or a family code word) trips up impostors. Then call him directly to be sure.

options.label: Stay on the line and keep listening
options.feedback: Every extra minute on the call is what they're after — it's how the pressure builds. Hanging up costs nothing.

redFlags: Cash by courier, wire, crypto, or gift cards
A voice alone is no longer proof — AI can clone it
safestAction: Hang up and call your loved one on a number you know. Consider a family code word for emergencies.

followUps.setup: Twenty minutes later a man in a polo shirt is at your door for the envelope. Your phone buzzes.

content.body: The judge added a court processing fee of $1,500. Please give the courier the additional amount now or he cannot file tonight and your grandson stays until Monday.

followUps.prompt: He's waiting on the porch. What do you do?

options.label: Add the $1,500 so he isn't stuck all weekend
options.feedback: The fee that appears at the door is the whole design. Couriers collecting cash for “bail” are a scam every single time.

options.label: Shut the door and call your grandson's actual number
options.feedback: He answered on the second ring, at home. Hard in the moment, right every time.

options.label: Ask the courier for ID before handing anything over
options.feedback: He had a convincing badge — they always do. ID at your door proves nothing; the phone call to your family does.

title: Online sweetheart needs help with a fee
setup: For three months you've messaged daily with someone you met on a dating app. He says he's a doctor working overseas. You've never video chatted — his camera is “broken.”

messages.text: My contract ends next week and I can finally come home to you, my love.
But customs is holding my gold and belongings until I pay a $2,500 clearance fee. My accounts are frozen here. Could you help? I will repay you the moment I land. 🙏

options.label: Send the $2,500 — you trust him
options.feedback: There was always another fee after this one. “James” was a scammer using stolen photos.

options.label: Refuse, and talk it over with a friend or family member
options.feedback: Anyone you've never met in person who asks for money is a scammer. An outside view makes that easier to see.

options.label: Send half to show you care
options.feedback: Any money proves you'll pay, and the requests grow from there.

redFlags: Never met in person; avoids video calls
Works overseas: military, oil rig, doctor
Sudden money emergency, promises to repay
safestAction: Never send money to someone you've only met online. Do a reverse image search on their photos.

title: Sister requests her share of Mom's gift
setup: On a family call yesterday, you and your sister agreed to split Mom's birthday gift. She said she'd send a request.

options.label: Pay it
options.feedback: You agreed on this, it's her usual account, and the amount matches. That's a real request.

options.label: Decline and block — could be a hacker
options.feedback: Being careful is good, but this matched your plan exactly. A quick text to her would have confirmed it.

redFlags: Matches something you already agreed to
safestAction: When a request matches a real plan with someone you know, it's fine. When in doubt, confirm by calling or texting them directly.

title: “Hi Mom, this is my new number”
setup: You get a text from an unknown number. Your adult daughter lives in another city.

messages.text: Hi Mom it's me, I dropped my phone in the sink 🤦‍♀️ this is my new number, save it!
Ugh I'm locked out of my banking app on the new phone and my rent payment of $1,850 is due today. Can you pay it for me? I'll pay you back Friday. Can't talk, at work

options.label: Pay the rent so she isn't late
options.feedback: Your daughter's phone was fine. The “landlord's account” belonged to a scammer.

options.label: Call her old number to check
options.feedback: Calling the number you've always had reaches the real person. She was surprised and fine.

options.label: Text back a question only she'd know
options.feedback: Scammers can't answer personal questions. Then call her old number to be certain.

redFlags: “Can't talk right now” to avoid a call
safestAction: Call your family member on the number you already have before sending anything.

title: Old friend posts about crypto profits
setup: A college friend, whose account you've followed for years, messages you directly.

messages.text: Hey!! Long time 💕 I have to tell you, I just got a $15,000 payout from an investment program my coworker showed me. Totally legit, I was skeptical too.
Here's my screenshot. They're only taking a few more people. Want me to connect you with my account manager?

options.label: Get connected — it's Jess, you trust her
options.feedback: Jess's account had been hacked. The “account manager” took your deposit and vanished.

options.label: Call or text Jess outside the app to ask if it's really her
options.feedback: She had no idea — her account was hacked. You checked and warned her too.

options.label: Ask her more questions in the chat
options.feedback: The hacker replies as Jess, using details from her old messages. The chat can't confirm anything.

redFlags: “Only a few spots left” and an “account manager”
safestAction: If a friend suddenly pitches money-making online, contact them another way. Their account may be hacked.
